title: Burnside's Lemma
short: The number of orbits is the average number of points fixed by a group element; count necklaces and colorings up to symmetry by adding up the fixed colorings over the group.
trouble: Students divide the total number of colorings by |G|, which works only when no coloring is fixed by anything except e.

blocks.html: How many different necklaces can you make with 6 beads in 2 colors, if turning a necklace does not change it? There are $2^{6} = 64$ colorings, and the rotations group them into orbits; the question asks for the number of orbits. Dividing by the number of rotations fails, because orbits have different sizes. Burnside's lemma counts them correctly.

Burnside's lemma. If a finite group $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, the number of orbits is $$\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)|, \qquad \mathrm{Fix}(g) = \{x : g \cdot x = x\}.$$ Proof. Count the pairs $(g, x)$ with $g \cdot x = x$ in two ways. By $g$: $\sum_{g} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)|$. By $x$: $\sum_{x} |G_{x}|$, and by orbit–stabilizer $|G_{x}| = |G|/|G \cdot x|$. So $$\sum_{g} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)| = |G| \sum_{x} \frac{1}{|G \cdot x|}.$$ The points of one orbit $O$ contribute $|O| \cdot \frac{1}{|O|} = 1$, so the last sum is the number of orbits. $\square$

Counting fixed colorings. A coloring is fixed by a symmetry exactly when the symmetry never moves a bead onto a bead of a different color, that is, when each cycle of the symmetry (as a permutation of the beads) is a single color. With $k$ colors and $c$ cycles, $k^{c}$ colorings are fixed. Rotating $n$ beads by $j$ steps has $\gcd(n, j)$ cycles.

blocks.name: aa-burnside

opts.task: Pick each rotation in turn and count its cycles, then open the Burnside table.

blocks.cap: Rotating a 6-bead necklace by 2 steps makes 2 cycles (rings of the same color), so $2^{2} = 4$ colorings are fixed. The table averages the fixed counts over all six rotations.

blocks.title: Necklaces with 6 beads
blocks.q: Count 6-bead necklaces in 2 colors, up to rotation.

blocks.title: Corners of a square
blocks.q: Color the 4 corners of a square with 2 colors. How many colorings are there up to rotations and reflections ($D_{4}$)?
steps: $e$: $2^{4} = 16$. Quarter turns $r, r^{3}$ (one 4-cycle): $2$ each. Half turn (two 2-cycles): $4$.
Diagonal mirrors (two fixed corners, one 2-cycle): $2^{3} = 8$ each. Side mirrors (two 2-cycles): $4$ each.

blocks.title: Painting a cube
blocks.q: Paint each face of a cube one of 2 colors. How many different cubes are there, up to rotation?
steps: The $24$ rotations by type, with their cycles on the faces: identity ($6$ cycles); $6$ quarter turns about face axes ($3$ cycles); $3$ half turns about face axes ($4$); $8$ turns about vertex axes ($2$); $6$ half turns about edge axes ($3$).

blocks.html: Dividing the total number of colorings by $|G|$: $64/6$ is not even a whole number. That shortcut assumes every orbit has $|G|$ members, which fails whenever some coloring is fixed by a symmetry other than $e$ (the one-color necklaces are fixed by everything). Burnside's average of fixed counts is always a whole number; if yours is not, recount the cycles.
Number of orbits = average number of fixed points: $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)|$. For colorings, a symmetry with $c$ cycles fixes $k^{c}$ of them.
